'''JoAnne Stubbe''' (born June 11, 1946) is an American chemist best known for her work on [[ribonucleotide reductase]]s, for which she was awarded the [[National Medal of Science]] in 2009. In 2017, she retired as a professor of chemistry and biology at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://chemistry.mit.edu/chemistry-news/lippard-and-stubbe-honored-with-retirement-reception/|title=Lippard and Stubbe Honored with Retirement Reception – MIT Department of Chemistry|date=27 October 2017 |language=en-US|access-date=2019-06-29}}</ref>

==Career and education==
In 1946, Stubbe was born in Champaign, Illinois.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last=Iii and Potuzak|date=2014|title=The 2010 Benjamin Franklin meal in chemistry presented to JoAnne Stubbe|journal=Journal of the Franklin Institute}}</ref> In 1968, Stubbe received a B.S. degree in [[chemistry]] from the [[University of Pennsylvania]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://biology.mit.edu/profile/joanne-stubbe/|title=JoAnne Stubbe|website=MIT Department of Biology|language=en-US|access-date=2019-06-29}}</ref> and worked as an undergraduate in the laboratory of Professor Edward R. Thornton.<ref name=":3" /> After she received her Ph.D. degree in [[organic chemistry]] under the guidance of Professor George Kenyon<ref name=":3" /> from the [[University of California, Berkeley]], in 1971, she did a very brief stint (1971–1972) as a postdoc at UCLA, where she worked on synthesizing LSD from tryptophan with [[Julius Rebek]]. Then, Stubbe taught at [[Williams College]] (1972–1977) discovered she didn't want to teach, but wanted to do research. Her realization sent her to [[Brandeis University]] (1975–1977),<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://news.mit.edu/2011/killian-stubbe-0518|title=Stubbe wins faculty's Killian Award|website=MIT News|date=19 May 2011 |access-date=2016-01-28}}</ref> where she did a second postdoc with [[Robert Abeles]]. This is where she learned the art and science of creating mechanism-based [[enzyme inhibitor]]s.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last=Hopkin|first=K|date=2007|title=JoAnne Stubbe – Making life possible|journal=The Scientist}}</ref> She also taught at [[Yale School of Medicine]] (1977–1980) as an assistant professor in the department of [[pharmacology]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=http://www.chem.uzh.ch/static/events/dch/2008/Stubbe.html|title=DCH 2008|website=www.chem.uzh.ch|access-date=2016-04-13}}</ref>

In 1980, she moved to the [[University of Wisconsin]], serving as assistant professor in the [[Biochemistry]] Department and rising to full professor in 1985.<ref name=":1" /> She was an assistant professor for a total of 12 years.<ref name=":2" /> In 1987, Stubbe became a professor in the [[MIT Chemistry Department]], where she became the first woman to receive tenure in that department.<ref name="Johnson">{{Cite news|url=http://archive.boston.com/news/local/massachusetts/articles/2009/09/18/white_house_to_give_mit_scientist_top_honor/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190629183003/http://archive.boston.com/news/local/massachusetts/articles/2009/09/18/white_house_to_give_mit_scientist_top_honor/|url-status=dead|archive-date=June 29, 2019|title=White House to give MIT scientist top honor|last=Johnson|first=Carolyn Y.|date=2009-09-18|work=Boston.com|access-date=2019-06-29}}</ref> She received a joint appointment in the [[MIT Department of Biology|MIT Biology Department]] in 1990.

In 1994, Stubbe was one of 16 women faculty in the School of Science at MIT who drafted and co-signed a letter to the then-Dean of Science (and later Chancellor of Berkeley) Robert Birgeneau, which started a campaign to highlight and challenge gender discrimination at MIT.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Zernike |first=Kate |title=The Exceptions: Nancy Hopkins, MIT, and the Fight for Women in Science |publisher=Scribner |year=2023 |isbn=978-1-9821-3183-8 |location=New York, NY}}</ref>

== Research ==
Stubbe has published over 300 scientific papers and has been frequently recognized for her research achievements.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/pressroom/newsreleases/2019/june/acs-names-joanne-stubbe-2020-priestley-medalist.html|title=American Chemical Society names JoAnne Stubbe 2020 Priestley Medalist|website=American Chemical Society|language=en|access-date=2019-06-29}}</ref> Before Stubbe's work, there were no [[Reaction mechanism|chemical mechanisms]] that could be written for certain enzymes. She revolutionized the [[biochemistry]] field with her first two scientific papers on enzymes [[enolase]] and [[pyruvate kinase]].<ref name=":2" />

Her first two publications in scientific journals showed the mechanisms for reactions that involved the enzymes enolase that [[Metabolism|metabolizes]] [[carbohydrate]]s, and pyruvate kinase.<ref name=":1" /> Her first groundbreaking experiments were carried out in the late 1970s and early 1980s, while she was at Yale, then the University of Wisconsin. She was trying to understand how the [[Hydroxyl|hydroxyl group]] at the 2' position of the [[ribonucleotide]]'s sugar was replaced by the [[hydrogen]] found in [[deoxyribonucleotide]]s. To perform these experiments, she had to synthesize nucleotides that carried a heavy [[isotope]] at specific positions. Stubbe reportedly kept a bed in her office since she worked around the clock on her experiments.<ref name=":2" /> Stubbe pioneered the use of [[Spectrometer|spectroscopic]] investigations of [[enzyme]] interactions<ref>{{Citation|date=9 February 2009|pages=41–42|title=Nakanishi Prize|journal=Chemical & Engineering News}}</ref> and has devoted most of her career to elucidating the biochemical mechanisms behind [[free radicals]]. In her early work at Yale and then at the University of Wisconsin, Stubbe discovered how enzymes called ribonucleotide reductases use free-radical chemistry to convert [[nucleotide]]s into deoxynucleotides, an essential process in [[DNA repair]] and [[DNA replication|replication]].<ref>{{Cite web|title = Making Life Possible {{!}} The Scientist Magazine|url = http://www.the-scientist.com/?articles.view/articleNo/24706/title/Making-Life-Possible/|website = The Scientist|access-date = 2016-01-28}}</ref> These enzymes catalyze the [[rate-determining step]] in DNA biosynthesis. Her analysis of the nucleotide reduction process shed light on the mechanism of action of the Eli Lilly & Co. anti-cancer drug [[gemcitabine]], which is used to treat various [[carcinoma]]s, such as [[pancreatic cancer]], [[breast cancer]], and non-small cell [[lung cancer]].<ref name=":0" />

Stubbe, in collaboration with John Kozarich, also elucidated the structure and function of [[bleomycin]], an antibiotic that is commonly used to treat cancer. They discovered how bleomycin induces DNA strand breaks in tumor cells, which in turn induces [[apoptosis]].<ref name=":0" />

Before retiring, Stubbe studied the function of ribonucleotide reductases and the mechanisms of clinically useful drugs. She also extended her research into [[polyhydroxybutyrate]]s, a class of biodegradable [[polymer]]s that can be synthesized by bacteria under certain conditions and then converted into plastics.<ref>{{Cite web|title = JoAnne Stubbe Research Group – MIT|url = http://web.mit.edu/biochemistry/research.htm|website = web.mit.edu|access-date = 2016-01-28}}</ref> Stubbe's other research interests included the design of so-called [[Suicide inhibition|suicide inhibitors]] and mechanisms of DNA repair enzymes.<ref name=":1" />

Stubbe was active on several committees, including review boards for the [[National Institutes of Health|NIH]] grants committee and the editorial boards for various scientific journals.<ref name=":1" />

== Personal life ==
Stubbe's parents were teachers, and that is why she thought teaching is what she originally wanted to do as a career.<ref name=":2" /> Stubbe had a pet dog named Dr. McEnzyme Stubbe. The dog was a part of the research group and had its own email address and picture on the group's website.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://harvardmagazine.com/2013/05/honorary-degree-recipients|title=Abreu, Menino, Pagels, and Oprah: The Honorands|date=2013-05-30|website=Harvard Magazine|language=en|access-date=2020-01-29}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://web.mit.edu/biochemistry/people.htm|title=JoAnne Stubbe Research Group – MIT|website=web.mit.edu|access-date=2020-01-29}}</ref>
